title: Visiting
hook: many Jews visit services unlike their own and learn from them

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: love your fellow. Ahavat Yisrael, tested by the Jew unlike you. Did you take your small step across a divide? Today, a step you can take with your feet. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

A guest slips into the back row of a synagogue that isn't hers. Within five minutes she is lost. The melody for a prayer she has sung all her life is a different melody. Nobody announces page numbers. Everyone stands at a moment she would have sat, and faces a direction she didn't expect. A kind stranger leans over and points to the line. By the end she has learned a tune she'll hum for a week, and noticed something about her own synagogue she never saw from inside it. She was a visitor. Today's word is what she did.
screen: `THE BACK ROW.` → `A DIFFERENT MELODY.` → `A STRANGER POINTS TO THE LINE.`

segments.voice: Visiting. Turn it four ways. First, the teaching behind it. In the Mishnah, Ben Zoma asks: who is wise? And answers: the one who learns from every person. Not from every teacher. From every person. A visitor walks in as a learner, which is the posture Ben Zoma calls wise. Second, what you might find. Some synagogues seat men and women apart, with a partition called a mechitza. Some sit together. Some pray almost entirely in Hebrew, quickly, each person at their own pace. Some sing slowly, in Hebrew and English, with the whole room on one tune. Sephardi and Ashkenazi rooms may chant the same words to different melodies. None of these is the visitor's to grade. Each is somebody's home. Third, how to be a guest. Dress the way the room dresses. Follow the room's lead: stand when it stands, keep your phone away where that is the custom. Say less, watch more. Save your questions for afterward, over the cake, when people may be glad to explain. Fourth, what comes home with you. Visitors bring back a melody, a custom, a phrase. They also bring back their own synagogue, seen fresh, the way a trip abroad makes your own kitchen look new. Hosts have their side too: hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, a value the tradition traces to Abraham running from his tent to greet strangers. A good visit needs a learner at the door and a welcome inside it.
screen: `WHO IS WISE? WHO LEARNS FROM EVERYONE.` · `EACH ROOM IS SOMEBODY'S HOME.` · `SAY LESS, WATCH MORE.` · `YOUR OWN ROOM, SEEN FRESH.` · then, large: `VISIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit a different kind of service, even online. Settle, and breathe. Think of a kind of service you've never been to, or haven't been to in years. Another stream, another community, another style. Some congregations stream their services online. Choose one. Then choose one thing to watch for when you visit: a melody, a gesture, the way people greet each other at the door. If you pray, you can ask to be a good guest. If you don't, just hold the plan. The bell holds the time.
Visiting. Going to a service unlike your own as a learner and a guest, and coming home with something new. Today's word.
Your line: visit. Today, find the service you chose and put it on your calendar, in person or on a screen. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews visit synagogues of other streams and styles while traveling, for a friend's celebration, or to learn, following the local customs of dress and seating and asking questions after the service.
